name: Repeated Bare Noun with a Preposition
pattern: Nᵢ + P + Nᵢ, with bare noun forms and a choice of preposition tied to the reading

entry.name: Repeated Bare Noun with a Preposition
entry.pattern: Nᵢ + P + Nᵢ, with bare noun forms and a choice of preposition tied to the reading

1.definition: Presents successive instances over an interval.
1.details: After presents a succession of distinct instances of one kind. CGEL also gives upon in mile upon mile. Nominal uses such as flight after flight of stairs coexist with adjunct uses. The construction's interpretation and the question of what heads each subtype can be evaluated separately.

examples.note: An NP use discussed by CGEL in the chapter on prepositions.

2.definition: Presents a process in successive units with by.
2.details: The repeated noun supplies the units by which an event proceeds. Which prepositions can express a particular reading is a property of the subtype. This entry records the productive succession patterns.

examples.note: The process advances by successive mouthfuls.

examples.form: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].
examples.note: Constructed test of the stepwise reading with a different noun.

relatedConstructions.notes: From N to N can relate two different nouns that restrict the endpoints.

grounds.note: Documents distinct readings by preposition and distinct nominal and adjunct distributions.

projection.target: The preposition and the matched noun slots together distinguish iteration over instances from a description of how an event proceeds.
projection.evidence: CGEL's matched forms and distributional contrasts. Jackendoff documents productive subtypes and lexical exceptions.

curious.title: The same noun twice with a word between
curious.summary: Repeating a noun around a small word, as in day after day, shows a series of separate instances or a job done in stages.
curious.body:
Say a noun, put after in the middle, say the noun again, and you get a long stretch made of one thing following another: day after day, flight after flight of stairs. The little word matters. With by the sense changes to a task done in steps, as in mouthful by mouthful.

The pattern lets a phrase work in more than one role. Flight after flight of stairs acts like a noun phrase, while others work as add-ons to a sentence. Which little word fits depends on which of the two meanings you want. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].

curious.try: Pick a noun, say it twice with after between, and put it in a sentence. Then try by in the middle. Does the picture change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain N after N (a succession of instances) and N by N (a process in stages).
teacher.explain: The pattern repeats a bare noun around a preposition. With after, it presents a succession of distinct instances of one kind (day after day); CGEL also gives upon in mile upon mile. With by, the repeated noun supplies the units by which an event proceeds (mouthful by mouthful). Which preposition can express a given reading is a property of the subtype, so teach the pairings as patterns. Some uses are noun phrases (flight after flight of stairs) and others are adjuncts. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].

contrasts.text: We checked the total invoice by invoice.
contrasts.note: The process advances in stages, one invoice at a time.

watch_for: A learner might use after where the by reading (a process in stages) is wanted.
A learner might repeat the noun in the plural, when the pattern as described here uses a bare noun form.
teacher.activity: Write nouns (page, step, drop, hour) on cards. Pairs make one N after N phrase and one N by N phrase with each noun in a sentence, then explain how the two sentences differ.

child.hook: What do we call it when one day follows another again and again?
child.explain: Say a word twice with after in the middle. Day after day means day, then another day, and another. With by it means doing something one piece at a time.

examples.text: She ate her dinner [mouthful by mouthful].

child.play: Pick a noun, like step or page. Make up a sentence with it twice around after. Then try it around by and see how the meaning changes.
